podcast.title: First All-Female Band with Critical and Commercial Success (1969-1975)
podcast.body: Formed in 1969 in Los Angeles, Fanny consisted of four women, including two from the Philippines. They are arguably the first all-female band to achieve both critical acclaim and commercial success before their breakup in 1975. "And you could make a case that this was the first all-female band to enjoy both critical and commercial success."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Documentary Feature - Fanny, The Right to Rock (2021)
podcast.body: Fanny's legacy and reputation continue to be recognized, evidenced by the highly recommended 2021 documentary "Fanny, The Right to Rock," which brought renewed attention to their pioneering contributions to music. "If you're interested in learning more, I highly recommend a 2021 documentary called Fanny, The Right to Rock."

podcast.title: "Fanny: The Right to Rock" Documentary

podcast.title: David Bowie's Endorsement
podcast.body: Despite their struggle for commercial success across four albums before disbanding in 1975, Fanny garnered high praise from David Bowie, who considered them "brilliant." "Like I said, Bowie thought they were brilliant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.title: Esteemed Fans and Original Songwriting
podcast.body: Before their breakup in 1975, Fanny garnered a significant following that included David Bowie, John Lennon, George Harrison, and Sly Stone. They released five major label albums and notably wrote all their own songs, a rare feat for female artists at the time. "David Bowie, John and George from The Beatles, Slice Stone, and a ton of other big names became huge fans. They released five major label albums and they wrote all their own songs, which is something almost no female artists did back in those days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Highly Respected by Famous Musicians
podcast.body: Fanny garnered a significant following among prominent musicians, with huge fans including David Bowie, John Lennon and George Harrison from The Beatles, and Sly Stone, among many other big names in the industry. David Bowie even sent them a fan letter and spoke highly of them in interviews. "Before they broke up in 1975, David Bowie, John and George from the Beatles, Slice Stone, and a ton of other big names became huge fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Image Expectations and Novelty Act Status
podcast.body: Fanny faced constant pressure to "sex it up" for their image, despite their preference for regular street clothes when performing live. Their original record deal itself was secured only because they were signed as a novelty act, underscoring the sexist industry attitudes they encountered. "Even their original record deal came about only because they were signed as a novelty act."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Future Female Artists
podcast.body: Although they lacked widespread commercial breakthrough, Fanny was "tremendously influential on other young women," inspiring future all-female or female-fronted bands that would achieve greater fame, including The Runaways, Heart, The Go-Go's, and The Bangles. "And although commercial success escaped them through four albums before they broke up in 1975, they were tremendously influential on other young women."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Proficiency and Collaboration with Barbra Streisand
podcast.body: The members of Fanny were highly skilled musicians, capable of working as studio musicians. In 1971, their talent was recognized when none other than Barbra Streisand hired them to appear on one of her albums, a testament to their professional caliber. "In 1971, no one less than Barbara Streisand hired them to appear on one of her albums."

podcast.title: Pioneering All-Female Rock Band
podcast.body: Fanny was an excellent all-female rock group from California that achieved significant milestones, including a major label deal with Warner. They were the third all-female group to secure such a deal, following Goldie and the Gingerbreads and The Pleasure Seekers. "With DeBure, they ended up with a major label deal with Warner, making them the third all-female group behind Goldie and the Gingerbreads and the Pleasure Seekers to have that kind of deal."

podcast.title: Pioneering All-Female Rock Band
podcast.body: Formed in Los Angeles in 1972, Fanny was an all-female rock band, a concept virtually unheard of at the time when it was commonly believed that "women couldn't rock," making their existence a significant challenge to prevailing gender norms in music. "Now at that time, the idea of an all-female rock band was unheard of. You just didn't do this. I mean, everybody knew that women couldn't rock, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.title: Pioneering Self-Songwriting and Touring
podcast.body: The band distinguished itself by writing all of its own songs, a rare feat for female artists of their time. They also toured with major acts such as Jethro Tull and Humble Pie, and their work influenced a generation of aspiring female rockers. "They released five major label albums, and they wrote all their own songs, which is something almost no female artists did back in those days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Breakup Careers
podcast.body: After Fanny broke up, original drummer Bray Brantz, who had returned for the band's fourth album, went on to tour and perform with several major artists including Elton John, ELO, Carole King, and Jimmy Buffett. This highlights her continued success despite the challenges Fanny faced. "But after they broke up, original drummer Brent Bray, who returned to the group for their fourth album, went on to tour and perform with Elton John, ELO, Carol King, and Jimmy Buffett, among others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

podcast.title: Reasons for Obscurity: Ahead of Their Time and Sexism
podcast.body: Despite their talent and success, Fanny's relative obscurity today is attributed to two main factors: they were considered ahead of their time, as the mainstream rock community was not ready for their innovation, and pervasive sexism, evident in dismissive attitudes like "you're pretty good for a girl." "First of all, they were ahead of their time. The mainstream rock community just wasn't ready for this kind of innovation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Session Work with Barbra Streisand
podcast.body: Proving their musical prowess, Fanny's members were skilled enough to work as studio musicians, even being hired by Barbra Streisand in 1971 to appear on one of her albums. "In 1971, no one less than Barbara Streisand hired them to appear on one of her albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sexism and Novelty Status
podcast.body: Despite their talent, the band faced considerable sexism, often being told they were "pretty good for a girl" and asked to "sex it up" for their image. Their initial record deal was secured under the premise of them being a "novelty act." "And their original record deal came about only because they were signed as a novelty act."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring and Influence
podcast.body: Fanny toured with prominent acts such as Jethro Tull and Humble Pie, and their work was instrumental in influencing a generation of aspiring female rock musicians. "They toured with big acts like Jethro Tull and Humble Pie and they influenced a generation of wannabe female rockers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Victims of Industry Sexism
podcast.body: Despite their talent and championship by figures like David Bowie, Fanny's career was hindered by the "old boys club" in the music industry. They were not given due credit as musicians and songwriters, instead being pressured to conform to expectations of being "cute" and "sexy," which they refused. "Unfortunately, Fanny became a victim of the old boys club in the recorded music industry, and weren't given their dues as musicians and songwriters."

xref.title: Formation and Inspiration (1975)
xref.body: The Runaways were formed by producer Kim Fowley, who was inspired by the success of the all-female band Fanny. Active from 1975 to 1979, they are arguably recognized as the first all-female hard rock band, featuring future stars Joan Jett and Lita Ford. "The first is to a weirdo producer named Kim Fowley, who was inspired by the group to form the Runaways, arguably the first all-female hard rock band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Family Connection to Fanny
xref.body: Suzi Quatro is the sister of Patty Quatro, who joined the band Fanny in 1974. "She had a sister named Susie, and Susie became a big deal in the UK, Europe, and Australia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Pioneering Hard Rock
xref.body: The Runaways were formed by producer Kim Fowley, who was reportedly inspired by the band Fanny. They are often considered the first all-female hard rock band, featuring notable members like Joan Jett and Lita Ford. "The first is to a weirdo producer named Kim Fowley, who was inspired by the group to form the Runaways, arguably the first all-female hard rock band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: International Star, North American Obscurity
xref.body: Suzi Quatro, sister of Fanny's Patty Quatro, achieved massive success in the UK, Europe, and Australia, selling over 50 million albums worldwide. Despite these staggering sales, she remains relatively unknown in North America, where she never attained the same star status. "She had a sister named Susie, and Susie became a big deal in the UK, Europe, and Australia, but never in North America, where she still isn't that well known, which is crazy since she sold over 50 million albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rivers Cuomo's Pizza Crust Habit
xref.body: During the band's early, poor days, Rivers Cuomo would save pizza crusts in a fanny pack to eat later, demonstrating the band's financial struggles. "They were so poor that Rivers would save pizza crusts in a fanny pack."
